O is marked between A and B, indicating that the binary stars make circular motion around the vicinity of their common center. Below, an arrow marks the distance between the two stars A and B as L. The problem statement gives m_A=29M, m_B=36M, M=2×10^30 kg, L=2×10^5 m, G=6.67×10^-11 N·m^2/kg^2. Treat the circular motion of the binary stars as an equivalent two-body Kepler circular orbit; the angular frequency satisfies ω^2=G(m_A+m_B)/L^3. The total mass of the two stars is m_A+m_B=(29+36)M=65×2×10^30 kg=1.3×10^32 kg. L^3=(2×10^5)^3=8×10^15 m^3. Therefore G(m_A+m_B)/L^3≈(6.67×10^-11×1.3×10^32)/(8×10^15)≈1.1×10^6 s^-2, so ω≈√(1.1×10^6)≈1.0×10^3 s^-1. The circular-motion frequency f=ω/(2π)≈1.6×10^2 Hz, and the order of magnitude is 10^2 Hz. The problem states that the gravitational-wave frequency and the circular-motion frequency are of the same order of magnitude, therefore the order of magnitude of the gravitational-wave frequency is approximately 10^2 Hz.
